style_when: scale is the story — a port, a refinery, a data centre hall, a rail yard, a skyline of cranes — and the reader needs to feel how big it is
prompt: Telephoto 200mm photograph of an unbranded wide-body air-cargo freighter parked at a cargo terminal loading bay, main-deck loader raised to its open cargo door, low golden sun raking hard from the right across the concrete apron, long cast shadows. Compressed perspective presses the aircraft against a warehousing wall behind it: dock doors, galvanised steel racks and stacked air cargo pallets layered tight to the roofline. Palette of graphite, weathered orange and steel blue; brushed aluminum fuselage skin, galvanised steel, concrete grey. Crystal-clear air, deep industrial contrast, deep focus front to back, asymmetric composition with the freighter commanding the left third and open sky above. Fine film grain, no people, no text, no logos.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, watermarks, logos
rationale: This is a capacity-and-scale story where two physical systems — air freight and warehousing — tighten against the planner at once, so telephoto compression is the perfect craft: it literally stacks and squeezes the freighter against the packed storage facility. The machine hero named by the headline (air deals) commands the frame in its real operating environment, and the loaded warehouse wall carries the second leg of the squeeze without needing a split screen.
cue: Both legs of the buffer-versus-expedite trade stopped being priceable
subject: An unbranded wide-body air-cargo freighter loading air cargo pallets at a cargo terminal loading bay, telephoto-compressed against a packed warehousing wall
core_thesis: Short-term air deals hit 60% of new air capacity contracts in the third quarter while warehousing capacity contracted at its fastest rate since March 2022 — both legs of the buffer-versus-expedite trade stopped being priceable in the same week.
core_conflict: The expedite leg (air freight, now sold only in three-month floating deals) versus the buffer leg (warehousing space shrinking while inventory rebuilds upstream) — a pincer that breaks the safety-stock math
composition: Asymmetric wide framing with the freighter commanding the left third, telephoto compression stacking the warehousing wall tight behind it, open sky as breathing room above
